deep.reconstruction:
Notation. Euler writes p^k = ζ(k) = Σ 1/j^k. The function name q^m stands for the non-strict double sum q^m = Σ_{k≥1} k^{-m} Σ_{j≤k} j^{-n}. In modern terms this is ζ(m,n)+ζ(m+n), with ζ(m,n)=Σ_{k>j} k^{-m} j^{-n}; equivalently it is the 'star' value ζ*(m,n). The weight ('exponens ordinis') is λ=m+n. On the previous page he set a(b) = C(a,b), the binomial coefficient.

Shorthand. In the displayed formulas a lone p^k with an odd upper index is shorthand for the product p^k·p^{λ-k} = ζ(k)ζ(λ-k). Thus the leading 'p^m' means ζ(m)ζ(n), which the text spells out as p^m·p^n. The braced coefficient over p^{2i+1} is C(2i, n-1) + C(2i, m-1).

What the page does. It finishes §36 and states §37: the closed-form evaluation of every double Euler sum of odd weight λ through ζ(λ) and products ζ(odd)ζ(even). It notes that the terms stop at p^{λ-2}.

Case I (m even):
q^m = ζ(m)ζ(n) + ½(1+C(λ,n))ζ(λ) ± Σ_{i=0}^{(λ-3)/2} [C(2i,n-1)+C(2i,m-1)] ζ(2i+1)ζ(λ-2i-1).

Case II (m odd; on the next page): the ζ(m)ζ(n) term is absent ('*'), the ζ(λ) coefficient is ½(1-C(λ,n)), and the bracketed sum carries the opposite sign.

On the next page Euler remarks that the next term of the pattern would carry the coefficient C(λ-1,n-1)+C(λ-1,m-1) = C(λ,n). Read with the correct sign and ζ(0)=-½, that would-be term reproduces the ½·C(λ,n)ζ(λ) part, so the pattern is internally coherent.

The problem served is the evaluation of 'series singulares' (double zeta / Euler sums). This is the founding result on double zeta values of odd weight. §38 (next page) explains why even weight fails.
errors:
Sign check. With p^{2i+1} read as ζ(2i+1)ζ(λ-2i-1), the bracketed terms as printed have the wrong sign in both cases.
- Case I needs '−': for m=2, n=1 this gives q^2 = ζ(2)ζ(1) + 2ζ(3) − ζ(1)ζ(2) = 2ζ(3), and for m=2, n=3, q^2 = 11/2 ζ(5) − 2ζ(2)ζ(3).
- Case II needs '+': for m=3, n=2, q^3 = 3ζ(2)ζ(3) − 9/2 ζ(5) ≈ 1.2657, whereas the printed '−' gives a negative value for a positive series.
The likely explanation is an orientation or sign convention for the products fixed earlier in the paper, or a sign slip carried over from the tables on p.183. Either way the formula as printed, read naively, is incorrect in sign.
For n=1 or m=1 the formula formally contains the divergent ζ(1). It only makes sense as a cancellation between the leading product and the i=0 term; Euler does not comment on this here.

ideas.what: Reduction of every double Euler sum Σ k^{-m} H_k^{(n)} of odd weight m+n to ζ(m+n) and products ζ(odd)ζ(even), with explicit binomial coefficients
ideas.modern_name: Euler's evaluation theorem for double zeta values of odd weight (Euler–Borwein–Girgensohn formula)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E477, 1775/76); modern proofs by Borwein–Borwein–Girgensohn (1995) and others
ideas.where_published: E477, Novi Comment. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 20 (1776), §§36–37; widely cited in the multiple zeta value literature

ideas.what: Parity dichotomy: odd weight is reducible, while even weight is not reducible by these methods (stated in §38)
ideas.modern_name: Parity theorem for multiple zeta values (depth 2 case)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (observation); general parity theorem by Tsumura and by Ihara–Kaneko–Zagier

ideas.what: Pattern continuation: the next term's coefficient sums to C(λ,n), consistent with a ζ(0)=-1/2 term
ideas.modern_name: Boundary term of the shuffle/stuffle-derived formula

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known odd-weight double zeta formula, a standard cited origin of multiple zeta values. The only noteworthy point is the apparent sign inconsistency of the printed bracket terms, which is minor and probably known to the editors and later commentators.
transcription_corrections: Case I first term: the image reads 'q^m = p^m + ½(1+λ(n))p^λ ...', i.e. Euler writes just 'p^m' (shorthand for p^m·p^n), not 'p^m·p^n'.
The product line in the image appears as 'p^m=p^n=(...)(...)' because of a blurred dot; the intended reading 'p^m·p^n = (...)(...)' in the transcription is correct.
On the next page '½(1−λ)(n)' should read '½(1−λ(n))'.
